elements.element: Customer may assign without consent to an affiliate.
elements.evidence: The successor carve-out does not cover assignments to Customer affiliates, so the original consent requirement continues to apply.

elements.element: Customer may assign without consent to a successor in a merger.
elements.evidence: The added carve-out expressly permits either party to assign to a successor in a merger without consent, upon written notice.

elements.element: Customer may assign without consent to a successor in an acquisition.
elements.evidence: The added carve-out expressly permits either party to assign to a successor in an acquisition without consent, upon written notice.

elements.element: Customer may assign without consent to a successor in a sale of substantially all of its assets.
elements.evidence: The added carve-out expressly permits either party to assign to a successor in a sale of substantially all of its assets without consent, upon written notice.

elements.element: Every Vendor assignment requires Customer's consent.
elements.evidence: The mutual successor carve-out permits Vendor to assign in a merger, acquisition, or substantially-all-assets sale without Customer's consent.

elements.element: Customer may not unreasonably withhold consent to a Vendor assignment.
elements.evidence: For assignments requiring consent, the clause expressly provides that consent will not be unreasonably withheld.

elements.element: Vendor may never assign to a Customer competitor, regardless of consent.
elements.evidence: There is no competitor prohibition, and the successor carve-out could permit an assignment to a Customer competitor without consent.

elements.element: Vendor has no termination right upon Customer's change of control.
elements.evidence: The supplied operative language grants no termination right arising from Customer's change of control.

elements.element: Customer may assign to a transaction successor without Vendor's consent.
elements.evidence: The carve-out permits either party, including Customer, to assign to a successor in a merger, acquisition, or sale of substantially all assets without consent.

elements.element: Customer must provide Vendor written notice of an assignment to a transaction successor.
elements.evidence: The carve-out conditions the permitted assignment on written notice to the other party.

elements.element: Vendor may assign to a transaction successor without Customer's consent.
elements.evidence: The carve-out permits either party, including Vendor, to assign to a successor in a merger, acquisition, or sale of substantially all assets without consent.

elements.element: Vendor must provide Customer written notice of an assignment to a transaction successor.
elements.evidence: The carve-out conditions the permitted assignment on written notice to the other party.

elements.element: Customer assignments other than permitted successor assignments require Vendor's consent.
elements.evidence: The original mutual prior-written-consent requirement remains operative for assignments outside the successor carve-out.

elements.element: Vendor may not unreasonably withhold consent to other Customer assignments.
elements.evidence: The clause states that the required consent will not be unreasonably withheld.

elements.element: Vendor assignments other than permitted successor assignments require Customer's consent.
elements.evidence: The original mutual prior-written-consent requirement remains operative for assignments outside the successor carve-out.

elements.element: Customer may not unreasonably withhold consent to other Vendor assignments.
elements.evidence: The clause states that the required consent will not be unreasonably withheld.

result.reason: The redline fully implements the fallback through a mutual transaction-successor carve-out conditioned on written notice while retaining the not-unreasonably-withheld consent standard for other assignments. It does not satisfy the preferred position because Customer receives no affiliate carve-out, Vendor receives a consent-free successor carve-out, and there is no prohibition on assignments to Customer competitors. The change is targeted and does not disturb unrelated terms, though drafting quality is slightly reduced by framing an acquisition generically as having a 'successor' and by not defining the notice timing more precisely.
